cls.function: A bill to add a warrant rule to federal criminal law and a right to sue federal officials
cls.banner: The Surveillance Accountability Act is a bill in Congress. It is not law. If passed, it would change laws we already have. The government would need a warrant, which is permission from a judge, before it searches people. It would also need one before it gets their data from companies. And people could sue federal officials who break their Fourth Amendment rights. That part of the Constitution protects people from unreasonable searches.
cls.checks: Every type of check was run on this surveillance bill. The bill changes laws that already exist. So the review looked first at how it fits with those laws. That means their definitions and the ways people can enforce them.
purpose.ladder.mechanism: The bill would require a warrant, which is permission from a judge, before the government searches people. It would also require one before the government gets their data from companies. And it would let people sue federal officials.
purpose.ladder.outcome: The bill aims to protect Americans' personal data. The government could get that data only if a judge says yes.
purpose.ladder.aim: The bill's larger goal is to end mass surveillance by the government without warrants from judges. Mass surveillance means watching large numbers of people at once.
promises.0.p: Representative Thomas Massie put out a press release. It says the bill would require a warrant from a judge for every government search.
promises.0.why: The bill states its warrant rule in broad terms. But it never says which agencies count as "the government". It ties the meaning of "search" to a test that courts made. Several of its definitions cover only searches aimed at one "specific" person. And it does not say how it fits with older surveillance laws.
promises.1.p: Representative Lauren Boebert put out a press release. It says the bill would cover both federal and local agencies.
promises.1.why: The bill uses the words "the government" and "a government entity". An entity is a group or body. The bill does not say if states, cities and counties count. Its new right to sue covers only people acting under federal law.
promises.2.p: The sponsors say the bill would close a gap in the law. That gap lets the government get data people share with companies without a warrant.
promises.2.why: The bill does ban the government from getting data that companies hold without a warrant, which is permission from a judge. But it lets the government skip the warrant when someone gives consent. It never says whose consent counts. It skips the warrant for public information too. And its meaning of "search" uses the same court test that made the gap.
promises.3.p: Representative Lauren Boebert put out a press release. It says the bill would stop federal agencies from buying location data that companies sell.
promises.3.why: The bill bars the government from getting "access" to data held by data brokers without a warrant. Data brokers are companies that collect and sell personal data. This ban would cover buying from them. But the bill never mentions buying, selling or contractors. It does not require anything of the companies that sell the data.
promises.4.p: Representative Thomas Massie put out a press release. It says the bill would stop the government from tracking people without a warrant. That includes tracking with face scans or license plate readers.
promises.4.why: The bill's part on face scans and plate readers is not a direct ban. It only limits the bill's exceptions to the warrant rule. And its wording can be read more than one way.
promises.5.p: Representative Lauren Boebert put out a press release. It says the bill would stop federal agencies from pushing local police to share data. This is data gathered without a warrant.
promises.5.why: The bill as first filed says nothing about federal and local agencies sharing data. It also says nothing about rules that come with federal grant money.
promises.6.p: The sponsors' press releases say the bill would let people sue for money when the government breaks their rights.
promises.6.why: The new right to sue covers rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment", meaning rights that part of the Constitution protects. It does not cover the bill's own new warrant rule. The bill also does not say if sued officials can use a common defense. Courts allow that defense under the older civil rights law the bill copies.
questions.0.q: The surveillance bill has a long full title. It promises warrants for searches that "significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person". Where do its rules use that phrase?
questions.0.a: The bill's actual rules never use that phrase. To "impinge" means to cut into. The rules define a search with a different test. They ask if a person had a "reasonable expectation of privacy", meaning a fair reason to expect privacy. A court comparing the title with the rules would follow the rules.
questions.1.q: The surveillance bill says "The government shall not access" people's data held by companies. Which governments does that mean?
questions.1.a: The bill does not say. Its new warrant rule would go into federal criminal law. Its new right to sue covers only people acting under federal law. One sponsor's press release says local agencies are covered. If the bill means to bind states, it would have to say so. It would also have to rely on a power the Constitution gives Congress.
questions.2.q: Who makes, holds, moves, sells and uses the personal data in the surveillance bill? At which step does the bill act?
questions.2.a: Apps, phone companies, banks and device makers collect the data. Data brokers, which are companies that trade in personal data, combine it and sell it. Agencies and their contractors buy it or demand it. The bill acts at only one step, when the government gets the data. It does not require anything of the companies that collect or sell it.
questions.3.q: Which government agencies have gotten people's data from companies without a warrant before? How did they defend it?
questions.3.a: In 2018 the Supreme Court required a warrant for phone location records held by cell phone companies. A warrant is permission from a judge. A Defense Intelligence Agency memo was made public in 2021. It said the agency bought location data from smartphones. The agency did not read the 2018 ruling to require a warrant for data it bought. A 2022 report went to the Director of National Intelligence, the head of the nation's spy agencies. It was once secret and is now public. It described spy agencies buying large amounts of data that companies sell.
questions.4.q: Say the surveillance bill stops agencies from getting people's data directly without a warrant. What is their next easiest way to get it?
questions.4.a: The bill leaves other ways to get data without a warrant, which is permission from a judge. An agency could use an older law that needs less proof. It could argue the new warrant rule did not cancel that law. It could collect data on everyone at once. Two of the bill's definitions of a search cover only a "specific" person. It could search data it already holds. The bill covers "acquisition and analysis" together, meaning getting and studying. It could rely on someone's "consent", or permission. It could treat bought data as public. Or it could have a contractor or partner agency hold the data.
questions.5.q: Which current laws let agencies get people's data from companies with less proof than a warrant? How does the surveillance bill treat them?
questions.5.a: Several laws let agencies do this. One is the Stored Communications Act. It allows court orders and subpoenas, which are legal demands for records. Others are FBI demand letters called national security letters, and a federal law on foreign spying. Banks must also file required reports. The bill mentions none of these laws. It does not say it overrides other laws. Courts avoid reading a new law as quietly canceling an older one. They usually say a specific law controls over a general one.
questions.6.q: If an agency breaks the surveillance bill's new warrant rule, what happens to it under the bill?
questions.6.a: The new warrant rule has no penalty of its own. Evidence would not be kept out of court, because the bill has no rule requiring that. The new right to sue covers breaking the Fourth Amendment. That is the part of the Constitution that bans unreasonable searches. It may not include acts that only the new rule forbids. An official who is sued can be expected to claim immunity, meaning protection from paying damages. Officials claim it under the older civil rights law too.
questions.7.q: The surveillance bill says "searches conducted with consent" need no warrant. Whose consent would count?
questions.7.a: The bill does not say. Consent means saying yes. One part says a company's consent cannot replace a warrant for data it holds about someone. Another part limits giving up the warrant right in a contract. But the consent exception itself has no limits.
questions.8.q: Who would gain and who would lose if the surveillance bill worked just as written?
questions.8.a: People whose data companies hold would gain a warrant rule. It would protect them from the government. The same data would still be collected and sold to private buyers. It could still leak or be stolen in data breaches. Investigators would lose tools they lawfully use today. That includes fraud, child exploitation and missing-person cases. Critics of the bill point to this trade-off.
questions.9.q: Would anyone have to report on, check or count how agencies search people's data under the surveillance bill?
questions.9.a: The bill would not require anyone to do so. It has no reporting rule and no audit, which is a formal check. It gives no role to an inspector general, the official who reviews an agency from inside. So Congress and the public would have no regular way to learn if searches without warrants from judges had stopped.
questions.10.q: What are the fewest changes that would make the surveillance bill do what its sponsors promised?
questions.10.a: The bill would need to say which governments it covers. It would need to let people sue when officials break the new warrant rule. It would need to say how it fits with older surveillance laws. It would need to say whose consent counts. It would need to cover bulk collection, meaning data gathered on many people at once. It would need to cover data agencies already hold. And it would need to keep evidence gathered by breaking the rule out of court. Ending the sale of this data altogether would take a separate rule aimed at sellers.
findings.S1.title: The bill never says which governments must get a warrant. State and local police might not be covered.
findings.S1.plain: The bill says "the government" may not get your data without a warrant, which is permission from a judge. It never says which governments it means. The words could reach every agency at every level. They could also be read to mean only federal law enforcement agencies.
findings.S1.tech: The bill uses "the government" and "a government entity" without defining them. An entity is a group or body. The warrant rule would go into federal criminal law. The right to sue covers only people acting under federal law. Both point toward federal agencies only. But one sponsor's press release says local agencies are covered. If the bill covers states, it would go further than the Constitution as courts read it. It would then need a power in the Constitution to bind them. That would likely be challenged in court.
findings.S1.use: A state or local agency could argue the bill's warrant rule does not apply to it. A federal agency could then get the same data from that state or local partner.
findings.S1.am.S1b.label: Define "government" with an open list that names the hard cases
findings.S1.am.S1b.cost: This change would define "government" with an open list. The list would name federal agencies, spy agencies, the military, states, local governments and contractors. Because the list stays open, other groups could still count. Naming states raises the question of how far Congress can bind state governments. The narrower option avoids that question.
findings.S1.am.S1a.label: Define "government" with a closed list
findings.S1.am.S1a.cost: This change would define "government" as a fixed list. The list would name federal agencies, their workers and contractors, and state or local bodies working with them. A fixed list makes things clear. But any body not on it would likely be left out. States would be covered only when they act with or for a federal agency. They would also be covered when they use federal money.
findings.S1.inq.q: What "the government" means decides which agencies the surveillance bill covers. Which real agencies would be in, and which would be left out?
findings.S1.inq.items.0.h: Florida's wildlife police ran license plate searches. They did this for the federal immigration agency.
findings.S1.inq.items.0.d: Audit logs are records of each search. They show that Florida's wildlife police ran license plate searches for the federal immigration agency. That agency is Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Each search checked more than 5,000 camera networks. The federal agency had no contract with the camera company. If "the government" means only federal agencies, the bill's warrant rule would not cover those state searches.
findings.S1.inq.items.1.h: Border Patrol agents have searched license plate data. Local police had gathered that data.
findings.S1.inq.items.1.d: Researchers at the University of Washington looked at Border Patrol. They found it ran hundreds if not thousands of searches of plate data from local police. The searches used a setting that let agents look up plates across the whole country. California's attorney general, the state's top lawyer, wrote to 20 police departments. The letters were about federal access. The attorney general also sued one of the departments.
findings.S1.inq.items.2.h: The surveillance bill does not say if military and spy agencies count as "the government".
findings.S1.inq.items.2.d: The Defense Intelligence Agency is a military spy agency. It made the location data purchases that became public. The new warrant rule would go into the part of federal law on crimes and police. The bill does not say if military and spy agencies count as "the government".
findings.S1.inq.items.3.h: The surveillance bill's new right to sue covers fewer officials than its new warrant rule does.
findings.S1.inq.items.3.d: The new right to sue covers only people acting under federal law. Say a state officer searches for a federal agency. That officer could be sued, if at all, only under the older civil rights law. That lawsuit would have to be for breaking the Constitution.
findings.S1.inq.open: No court has decided what "the government" means in this bill. Representative Boebert's press release says local agencies would be covered. But the bill's text does not say so.
findings.S1.two.dec: No agency is in charge of the surveillance bill, and only federal officials can be sued. So who first decides which agencies count as "the government"?
findings.S1.two.views.0.why: The sponsors would likely want local agencies named in the bill. One sponsor's press release says they are covered, but the bill's text does not say so.
findings.S2.title: The bill defines a "search" with the same court test that has let agencies get people's data without a warrant.
findings.S2.plain: The bill says a search is an act that intrudes on a "reasonable expectation of privacy". That means a fair reason to expect privacy. Courts used that same phrase to decide people expect no privacy in data they share with companies. The bill's title uses yet another standard. It covers searches that "significantly impinge" on privacy, meaning cut into it. That phrase appears nowhere in the bill's actual rules.
findings.S2.tech: Courts have held that people expect no privacy in facts they give a company. In 2018 the Supreme Court narrowed that rule for phone location records. The bill lists kinds of searches. It is unclear if they count on their own or must still pass the court test. The bill's separate ban on getting data from companies does not rely on this definition. Courts may look at a bill's title when its text is unclear. So the title's different phrase gives agencies another way to argue for a narrow reading.
findings.S2.use: Say an agency is sued for getting someone's data from a company. It could argue that was not a "search" at all, so no warrant was needed. A warrant is permission from a judge. The agency could also point to the bill's title to argue that only serious intrusions count.
findings.S2.am.S2a.label: Make the listed kinds of search count on their own
findings.S2.am.S2a.cost: This change would make the listed kinds of search count even if no court finds a privacy expectation. The bill also has a broad list of personal data. Together, almost any government handling of personal facts would become a search. That would raise pressure for clear exceptions to the warrant rule.
findings.S3.title: Two of the bill's three definitions of a search target one specific person. Mass data collection may fall outside them.
findings.S3.plain: Two of the bill's three definitions of a search cover acts aimed at a "specific" person. That means one certain person. Collecting data on everyone at once is not aimed at anyone in particular.
findings.S3.tech: The first definition covers acts "purposefully directed at a specific person or entity". An entity is a group or company. The second covers surveillance that "collects information on a specific individual or entity". Only the third, on personal data, lacks the word "specific". But it has its own limit. It covers "acquisition and analysis", meaning getting and studying data. The sponsors say the problem is bulk collection. That means gathering data on many people at once.
findings.S3.use: An agency could describe a mass data program as not aimed at anyone. It could then argue that the bill's rule requiring a warrant, which is permission from a judge, does not apply.
findings.S3.am.S3a.label: Name bulk data collection as a search
findings.S3.am.S3a.cost: This change would count collecting personal data in bulk, without aiming at one person, as a search. A warrant must describe exactly what is sought. So bulk collection would in practice be banned, not just limited. That would affect agencies that study large sets of data for reasons other than investigations.
findings.S4.title: The bill covers data that agencies both get and study. Searching data an agency already holds might not count.
findings.S4.plain: The bill covers the "acquisition and analysis" of personal data. That means getting it and studying it. Read strictly, an agency that searches data it already holds is studying it without getting it. So that search might not count.
findings.S4.tech: The word "and" normally means both things must happen. Another part of the bill lists "collection, retention, querying, or analysis" as separate acts. Those words mean collecting, keeping, searching or studying. That shows the drafters knew how to list them one by one. Searching data collected earlier is a central issue in today's debate over surveillance.
findings.S4.use: An agency could search data it gathered before the bill became law without a warrant, which is permission from a judge. It could do the same with data gathered under another law.
findings.S4.am.S4a.label: Count getting, keeping, searching or studying data separately
findings.S4.am.S4a.cost: This change would make getting, keeping, searching or studying personal data each count as a search. Keeping data would then be a search. So the bill would need a rule for data agencies already hold.
findings.S5.title: The bill lets the government skip a warrant for searches "with consent". It never says whose consent counts.
findings.S5.plain: Searches done "with consent", meaning when someone says yes, would need no warrant. A warrant is permission from a judge. The bill does not say whose consent counts. It could be the person the data is about. Or it could be the company holding the data.
findings.S5.tech: One part of the bill says a company's consent does not replace a warrant for data it holds. Another says a contract cannot give up the warrant right unless the user agrees in a "knowing, voluntary, and explicit" way. That means the user understands, chooses freely and says so clearly. But the bill's list of exceptions allows searches "with consent" with no limit. The bill does not say how these parts fit together.
findings.S5.use: A click-through agreement is fine print people accept by clicking a button. If it is labeled knowing and voluntary, it could count as the person's consent. The government could then claim that consent covers every search that follows.
findings.S5.am.S5a.label: Require consent from the person whose data it is
findings.S5.am.S5a.cost: This change would require consent from the person being searched, given for that search. Consent from a company or from fine print would not count. But companies sometimes have good reason to consent. One example is reporting a crime against the company using its own records. The bill might need a separate allowance for that.
findings.S6.title: The bill lets agencies use public information without a warrant. That holds even if someone else made it public.
findings.S6.plain: Information "made available by a person or entity to a public audience" would need no warrant. That means anything someone has shared with the public. A warrant is permission from a judge. The bill does not require that the person the information is about be the one who made it public.
findings.S6.tech: The public information exception covers anything shared "by a person or entity". That means anyone at all. Agencies have described data they bought as public or for sale. Another part of the bill limits this exception for data "exposed to public view or accessible to a third party". A third party is someone else, such as a company. But that limit applies only to data gathered in public places and a few similar settings.
findings.S6.use: An agency could treat data offered for sale to any buyer as public. It could then get that data without a warrant, which is permission from a judge.
findings.S6.am.S6a.label: Count only information people chose to make public about themselves
findings.S6.am.S6a.cost: This change would count information as public only in one case. The person it is about must have chosen to share it with the public for free. Narrowed that far, the government might need a warrant to read a news article about someone. The bill's separate exception for news outlets and public records would then have to cover that. So that exception should be checked too.
findings.S8.title: The bill's rule on face scans and plate readers is one unclear sentence. It may cover less than sponsors say.
findings.S8.plain: One sentence in the bill is meant to protect people from face scans and license plate tracking. It is long and has several conditions. It can be read to cover much less than the sponsors describe.
findings.S8.tech: This part of the bill only limits how the warrant exceptions are read. It is not a direct ban. It covers people who did not agree to data collection. That means collection in public places, on public roads or in businesses open to the public. The phrase "with respect to", meaning about, could limit only the consent part or the whole protection. The bill also lists face and plate data only as examples. So it is unclear if other data is covered.
findings.S8.use: An agency could argue that data gathered somewhere not listed falls outside the protection. One example is data from an online platform, such as a website or app.
findings.S8.am.S8a.label: Turn the face scan and plate reader limit into a direct ban
findings.S8.am.S8a.cost: This change would plainly ban collecting face or plate data without a warrant, however it was gathered. A flat ban would reach everyday uses, such as checking a plate during a traffic stop. The bill's exception for checking ID covers driver's licenses and other papers but not plates. So that case would need its own rule.
findings.S9.title: The bill says it does not limit police searches during "ordinary" encounters. It never says what makes one ordinary.
findings.S9.plain: The bill says nothing in it limits police searches "incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". That means searches that come up when police meet people in the normal course of their work. But the bill does not say what makes a meeting with police ordinary.
findings.S9.tech: This part keeps the power of police to hold, pat down and arrest people. It also keeps searches "incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". Courts already have a settled rule that allows searches during an arrest. The idea of searches during "ordinary encounters" is wider, and the bill never defines it. Officials could argue this part wins over the new warrant rule wherever the two meet.
findings.S9.use: Say an officer searches someone's phone at a routine stop. The officer could say the search was part of an ordinary encounter.
findings.S9.am.S9a.label: Allow only searches of a person during a lawful arrest
findings.S9.am.S9a.cost: This change would allow only searches of a person during a lawful arrest. It would not allow searches of what is on a phone or other device. That is narrower than what police do today in some settings. Police groups would object.
findings.S10.title: People could sue over breaking the Constitution's search protections. They could not sue over breaking the bill's own warrant rule.
findings.S10.plain: The bill creates a new warrant rule in one place and a right to sue in another. A warrant is permission from a judge. The right to sue covers breaking the Fourth Amendment, the part of the Constitution that bans unreasonable searches. It does not cover breaking the new rule. Where the new rule goes further than the Constitution as courts read it, there may be nothing to sue over.
findings.S10.tech: The right to sue covers losing rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment", meaning rights it protects. The new warrant rule is meant to require warrants where courts say the Constitution does not. Data held by companies is one example. Breaking the new rule without also breaking the Constitution would give no right to sue. The new rule has no penalty of its own either.
findings.S10.use: An agency could admit it broke the new warrant rule and still get the lawsuit thrown out. That is because no right in the Constitution was broken.
findings.S10.am.S10a.label: Let people sue over breaking the new warrant rule
findings.S10.am.S10a.cost: This change would let people sue when officials break the bill's own warrant rule, not only the Constitution. Federal workers could then be made to pay themselves under a new, untested rule. That would likely bring pressure to add a defense for officials who acted in good faith, meaning honestly.
findings.S10.inq.q: Which government acts would break the surveillance bill's new warrant rule but not the Constitution as courts now read it?
findings.S10.inq.items.0.h: Getting bank records with no warrant would break the surveillance bill's new rule. It would not break the Constitution.
findings.S10.inq.items.0.d: In 1976 the Supreme Court held that customers have no Fourth Amendment protection for records a bank holds. The Fourth Amendment is the part of the Constitution that bans unreasonable searches. The Court's 2018 Carpenter ruling said it did not change that. So getting bank records without a warrant would break the new rule but not the Constitution. The new right to sue would not apply.
findings.S10.inq.items.1.h: Getting records of phone calls and internet use with no warrant would break the surveillance bill's rule. It would not break the Constitution.
findings.S10.inq.items.1.d: The same is true of phone numbers dialed and similar records. A 1979 Supreme Court ruling covers them. The 2018 Carpenter ruling did not change that older ruling.
findings.S10.inq.items.2.h: The Supreme Court has not said if the Constitution guards data that the government buys from data sellers.
findings.S10.inq.items.2.d: The Supreme Court has not ruled on data the government buys. At least one agency has taken the view that the 2018 ruling does not require a warrant for bought data.
findings.S10.inq.items.3.h: The Supreme Court has not said if face scans or plate readers in public places are searches under the Constitution.
findings.S10.inq.items.3.d: The Supreme Court has not held that either one is a search. The bill tries to protect against both. But the new right to sue would not cover them.
findings.S10.inq.open: Lower courts disagree on some of these practices. When a court finds no search under the Constitution, the bill's right to sue would not apply.
findings.S12.title: The bill's rule on paying winners' lawyer fees points to "this Act". Inside older law, that phrase is unclear.
findings.S12.plain: The bill has a rule on lawyer's fees for people who win lawsuits. It covers suits "to enforce this Act". This rule would be added to an old collection of federal laws. There, "this Act" has no clear meaning.
findings.S12.tech: The fee rule would become new text inside the older collection of laws. Inside added text, "this Act" would usually be read to mean the law being changed. It would not mean the Surveillance Accountability Act. The fee rule for other civil rights lawsuits names the parts of law it covers by number.
findings.S12.use: The government, when sued, could fight paying the winner's lawyer's fees. It could argue the lawsuit enforced one part of the old laws, not an Act.
findings.S12.am.S12a.label: Point the lawyer's fee rule at the right part of the law
findings.S12.am.S12a.cost: This change would make the lawyer's fee rule clearly apply to lawsuits under the new right to sue. No cost of this change has been found.
findings.S13.title: The bill as first filed has four typing and wording mistakes. One is inside an exception to the warrant rule.
findings.S13.plain: The bill misspells "Definitions". It says "Searched conducted" where it means "Searches conducted". It says "new outlets" where it means "news outlets". It also leaves the word "is" out of one line that changes a current law.
findings.S13.tech: Three of the mistakes cause no harm. But "new outlets" is in an exception to the warrant rule. Someone could argue it means something other than news groups. The line missing "is" lacks the verb that makes it work.
findings.S13.use: Most of these mistakes would have little effect. But a mistake inside an exception to the warrant rule could end up argued over in court.
findings.S13.am.S13a.label: Fix all four mistakes
findings.S13.am.S13a.cost: This change would fix the four typing and wording mistakes. No cost of this change has been found.
findings.S15.title: Read word for word, the bill's warrant rule for company data covers routine bank and employer reports too.
findings.S15.plain: The bill bans the government from getting "any data" held by a company or other outside party without a warrant. Read word for word, that includes records agencies collect every day for other reasons than spying. Examples are reports that banks and employers must file.
findings.S15.tech: The ban is not limited to data about people. It is not limited to investigations either. Nor is it limited to data the government demands or buys. Required reports, government inspections and civil subpoenas all involve such data. Subpoenas are legal demands for records. When a rule is this broad, courts tend to read it narrowly to avoid upsetting other laws. That narrow reading could also cut into what the bill was meant to cover.
findings.S15.use: Agencies could point to how broad the ban is. They could ask courts to read it narrowly in every case.
findings.S15.am.S15a.label: Aim the ban at personal data wanted for investigations or spying
findings.S15.am.S15a.cost: This change would limit the ban to data about a person who can be identified. The data would also have to be wanted for police, spy or investigative work. But data gathered for routine government business could later be shared with investigators. So a rule on how the data may be used would be needed too.
findings.S7.title: The bill lets agencies skip a warrant in emergencies. It never defines an emergency or requires a later check.
findings.S7.plain: The bill lets agencies skip the warrant rule under "exigent circumstances", meaning emergencies. They would not need a warrant, which is permission from a judge. The bill does not say what counts as an emergency. It also does not require anyone to review the emergency claim afterward.
findings.S7.tech: The bill does not define "exigent circumstances", which means emergencies. So courts would use their existing rules on emergencies, which is a reasonable choice. Other surveillance laws allow emergency access too. But those laws make a court approve it afterward within a set time.
findings.S7.use: Agencies could start to use emergency access all the time if no one ever checks it.
findings.S11.title: The bill does not say if sued officials can use a defense that often ends lawsuits early.
findings.S11.plain: The new right to sue copies the wording of the main civil rights law. Under that law, courts let sued officials avoid paying damages unless the right was already clearly established. That means earlier court cases had already made the right clear. The bill does not say if that defense applies here.
findings.S11.tech: The new right to sue copies the main civil rights law. Courts let officials sued under that law use a defense called qualified immunity. A court would likely use that defense here too unless the bill says otherwise. For new surveillance tools, rights are rarely "clearly established" yet. The Supreme Court has sharply limited lawsuits against federal officers that courts created themselves. That is why a right to sue written by Congress matters, and why its details matter too.
findings.S11.use: Lawsuits for money could be thrown out early because of this defense. That could happen even when a violation really took place.
findings.S11.am.S11a.label: Block the defense and set a minimum payment
findings.S11.am.S11a.cost: This change would stop officials from arguing that the right was not clearly established. It would also set a minimum payment of $10,000 for each violation. Removing this defense for federal workers is disputed. Police and national security agencies would oppose it. Another option is to make the United States pay instead of the official.
findings.S16.title: The bill does not keep evidence out of court when it was gathered without a required warrant.
findings.S16.plain: The bill does not say that evidence found without a required warrant must be kept out of court. A warrant is permission from a judge. Keeping evidence out is the usual check on unlawful searches. That check would be missing for anything the bill adds beyond the Constitution.
findings.S16.tech: Keeping evidence out of court is a remedy for searches that break the Constitution. Sometimes only a law passed by Congress is broken. Then courts usually allow the evidence, unless that law says otherwise. The federal law on tapping phone calls is one law that does say otherwise.
findings.S16.use: The government could break the new warrant rule and still use the data it gathered against people. That includes criminal cases and other legal matters.
findings.S16.am.S16a.label: Keep evidence gathered in violation of the warrant rule out of court
findings.S16.am.S16a.cost: This change would bar using information gathered in violation of the warrant rule, or anything found through it, in court. That could end criminal cases because of unclear wording elsewhere in the bill. It makes every other wording problem in the bill more serious.
findings.S17.title: The bill does not say if its warrant rule wins over older laws that let agencies get data without warrants.
findings.S17.plain: A warrant is permission from a judge, given when there is probable cause. Probable cause means good reason to believe a crime occurred. Several laws already let agencies get data without such a warrant. Foreign intelligence law is one of them. The bill does not mention these laws or say that it wins if they conflict.
findings.S17.tech: The bill does not say how its warrant rule relates to other laws. It changes none of the laws on stored messages, FBI demand letters, foreign spying or bank reporting. Courts avoid reading a new law as quietly canceling an old one. And a specific law usually controls over a general one. The bill says it does not "authorize surveillance that would otherwise be unlawful", meaning illegal spying. It says nothing about surveillance that is otherwise lawful. The Senate's guide for bill writers says to name each conflicting law. It says a general override is unlikely to work.
findings.S17.use: An agency could keep using an older law written for a specific case. It could argue the general warrant rule left that law alone. For spy agencies, this is the most direct way around the bill.
findings.S17.am.S17a.label: Name the older laws the warrant rule overrides
findings.S17.am.S17a.cost: This change would name three laws and say the warrant rule overrides them. They are the Stored Communications Act, the FBI demand letter law and a foreign intelligence law. Any law not named would survive, so the list must be complete. This version leaves out bank reporting law and subpoenas issued without a court. Those would go on. The change would reshape how spy agencies collect data that affects Americans. It would also send the bill to more committees in Congress.
findings.S17.inq.q: Which laws let agencies get the kinds of data the surveillance bill covers without a full warrant from a judge?
findings.S17.inq.items.0.h: A foreign spying law lets agencies collect data on foreign targets without a warrant for each one.
findings.S17.inq.items.0.d: In 2022 this law on foreign spying covered nearly 250,000 targets. A court approved the program once a year, instead of a warrant for each target. That year the FBI ran roughly 119,000 searches of the collected data. The searches used details that identify Americans.
findings.S17.inq.items.1.h: The Stored Communications Act lets a judge order records handed over. It takes less proof than a warrant needs.
findings.S17.inq.items.1.d: The Stored Communications Act lets a court order records turned over based on "specific and articulable facts". That means facts that can be clearly stated. That is a lower standard than the probable cause a warrant needs. Probable cause means good reason to believe a crime occurred.
findings.S17.inq.items.2.h: The FBI can send letters to get customer records with no judge. They are called national security letters.
findings.S17.inq.items.2.d: A federal law lets the FBI demand records about a company's customers and their dealings with it. The FBI only has to approve its own request. No judge takes part.
findings.S17.inq.items.3.h: Banks must tell the Treasury Department when they see suspicious activity. No warrant is needed.
findings.S17.inq.items.3.d: A federal law makes banks report suspicious activity to the Treasury Department. So the government gets money data about named people with no warrant. It does not even have to ask.
findings.S17.inq.items.4.h: Many agencies can get business records with a subpoena, which is a legal order. No court is needed.
findings.S17.inq.items.4.d: Dozens of laws let agencies demand business records with no court involved. Drug cases are one example.
findings.S17.inq.items.5.h: Executive Order 12333, an order from the President, sets the rules for spying abroad.
findings.S17.inq.items.5.d: Spying abroad is done under the President's power, not under a law passed by Congress. The surveillance bill changes federal criminal law. It does not mention Executive Order 12333.
findings.S17.inq.open: The legal references for these powers are listed so readers can check them. But the laws themselves were not opened for this review. The 2022 figures are the newest that were checked.
findings.S17.two.dec: Is the surveillance bill meant to change how spy agencies collect data, or only how police do?
findings.S17.two.views.0.why: Intelligence and counterterrorism officials would like the bill to stay silent on their powers. That silence leaves their current powers in place.
findings.S17.two.views.1.why: Some members of Congress want to renew current surveillance law first. They would take up wider changes later.
findings.S17.two.views.2.why: A coalition of privacy and civil liberties groups wants agencies to get a warrant before they search spy data. It also wants to end government buying of data from brokers without a warrant.
findings.S18.title: The bill does not say when it would start or what happens to personal data agencies already hold.
findings.S18.plain: The bill does not say when it would take effect. It also does not say what happens to data agencies already have.
findings.S18.tech: With no start date, the bill would take effect as soon as it became law. It says nothing about keeping, deleting or still searching data gathered earlier. It also says nothing about investigations already under way.
findings.S18.use: Agencies could keep using the sets of personal data they already hold.
findings.S19.title: The bill does not require any reports or audits to show if agencies follow its new warrant rule.
findings.S19.plain: The bill has no reporting rule and no audit, which is a formal check. It gives no role to an inspector general, the official who reviews an agency from inside. So there would be no regular way to know if agencies had stopped searching without warrants.
findings.S19.tech: Surveillance laws often require yearly reports on court orders sought and granted. They also often require regular reviews by inspectors general. The right to sue depends on people learning they were searched. The bill does not require telling them.
findings.S19.use: People could not challenge searches that break the bill's warrant rule if no one ever tells them about those searches.
findings.S21.title: A sponsor says the bill stops federal pressure on local police to share data. The bill has no such rule.
findings.S21.plain: One sponsor's press release says the bill would stop federal agencies from pushing local police to share surveillance data. No such rule appears in the bill as first filed.
findings.S21.tech: The press release lists a ban on federal pressure on local police. The ban would cover data collected without a warrant. The bill says nothing about sharing data between governments or about rules tied to grants. It says nothing about fusion centers, which are shared federal and local intelligence offices. The ban may have been in an earlier draft.
findings.S21.use: People who read the press release could think the bill already deals with federal pressure on local police. But the bill has no rule on sharing data.
findings.S20.title: The bill limits government access to data from companies that sell personal data. It does not stop the sales.
findings.S20.plain: The bill tells the government not to get data from data brokers without a warrant. Data brokers are companies that sell personal data. A warrant is permission from a judge. The bill does not stop those companies from collecting or selling the data. The data would still exist. So any weak spot in the rule for government would leave the data open to it.
findings.S20.tech: Past cases show why this matters. A Defense Intelligence Agency memo, made public in 2021, described buying location data from companies. A 2022 report, once secret and now public, described spy agencies buying data from companies on a large scale. In 2025 Montana barred its own agencies from buying such data. In 2024 the House passed a bill aimed at government purchases from brokers. Neither ends the collection itself.
findings.S20.use: Any agency or partner the bill does not reach could still buy the data from data brokers.
findings.S20.am.S20a.label: Broader option: limit what data brokers may sell to governments
findings.S20.am.S20a.cost: This change would bar data brokers from selling personal data to any government body without a warrant. The Federal Trade Commission, which enforces rules on businesses, would enforce it. This goes beyond the bill's stated purpose. Limits on selling information face free speech challenges. The bill would need to define "data broker". And companies that collect data directly are not brokers. Banning data brokers altogether would go further. It would have larger effects on the economy and leave the same gap for companies that collect data themselves.
findings.S20.two.dec: Is the surveillance bill meant only to limit what personal data the government gets? Or is it meant to end the buying and selling of that data?
findings.S20.two.views.0.why: Data brokers and ad tech companies would prefer a rule aimed only at the government as a buyer. That would leave their business as it is.
bigger.issue: Protection from government searches in the digital age
bigger.lead: Suppose every part of the surveillance bill worked as intended. It would put a warrant rule on how the government gets data. A warrant is permission from a judge. For the reasons below, the bill would still not by itself end searches done without warrants.
bigger.map.0.part: Government access to personal data held by companies
bigger.map.0.note: The bill's main rule says the government needs a warrant to get data that companies hold. A warrant is permission from a judge.
bigger.map.1.part: Government purchases of personal data from data brokers
bigger.map.1.note: Buying data from brokers counts as "access" under the bill, meaning getting the data. But the bill never mentions buying or contractors.
bigger.map.2.part: Collection and sale of personal data by private companies
bigger.map.2.note: The bill does not require anything of companies that collect or sell personal data. The data stays open to other buyers, including foreign ones.
bigger.map.3.part: Foreign intelligence spying that collects Americans' data
bigger.map.3.note: Separate laws and the President's own power govern this spying. The bill never mentions them.
bigger.map.4.part: Older court orders, subpoenas and FBI demand letters that need less than a warrant
bigger.map.4.note: The bill does not say it overrides these older powers. It also does not change the laws that create them.
bigger.map.5.note: The bill does not define the words "the government". So it is unclear if the bill covers state and local agencies.
bigger.map.6.part: Government-run face scanning and license plate readers
bigger.map.6.note: The bill deals with face scans and plate readers only through a limit on its exceptions. How far that limit reaches is unclear.
bigger.map.7.part: Personal data that agencies already hold
bigger.map.7.note: The bill has no rule on data agencies already hold. It does not say if they may keep, delete or search it.
bigger.map.8.part: What happens when the warrant rule is broken
bigger.map.8.note: People could sue only over breaking the Constitution. Evidence would not be kept out of court. The bill says nothing about officials' immunity, meaning protection from paying damages.
bigger.map.9.part: Public reporting and oversight of government searches
bigger.map.9.note: The bill requires no reports, no audits and no notice to people who were searched.
stake.priv.want: Privacy and civil liberties advocates want a warrant rule with no gaps. They also want the government to stop buying people's data from data brokers.
stake.fle.want: Federal crime investigators want to get records fast, and lawfully, in cases of fraud, trafficking and missing people. Critics of the bill say warrant rules slow these cases down.
stake.ic.want: Intelligence and counterterrorism officials work on spying and on stopping terror attacks. They want to keep their foreign spy powers as they are.
stake.slp.want: State and local police want to keep using license plate readers and shared databases. They also want a clear answer on whether the warrant rule binds them.
stake.brok.role: Data brokers and ad tech companies
stake.brok.want: Data brokers and ad tech companies want to keep selling personal data. The government would be one customer among many.
stake.hold.want: Companies that hold customer data want a clear rule on when they must hand data to the government. They also do not want to be blamed for following it.
stake.surv.want: People who are watched the most want the same protection no matter which agency gets their data. News reports show local camera data reaching immigration agents.
stake.vict.want: Crime victims and those who speak up for them want investigations to move fast when someone is in danger.
stake.spon.role: Sponsors of the Surveillance Accountability Act
stake.spon.want: The bill's sponsors want a warrant for every government search. They describe the bill as covering federal and local agencies.
stake.opp.role: Members of Congress who want to renew current surveillance law first
stake.opp.want: Some members of Congress want current surveillance powers renewed first. They would leave wider changes for later.
stake.pl.role: Civil rights lawyers who would sue under the bill
stake.pl.want: Civil rights lawyers who would sue under the bill want a right to sue that courts will not throw out early.
stake.def.role: Government lawyers who would defend those lawsuits
stake.def.want: Government lawyers who would defend cases under the bill want each of its demands read as narrowly as they can.
stake.tex.role: A judge who follows a law's exact words
stake.tex.want: A judge who follows a law's exact words applies them as written. This judge will not fill in what Congress left out.
stake.pur.role: A judge who looks to a law's purpose
stake.pur.want: A judge who looks to a law's purpose settles doubts in favor of what the law was trying to do.
stake.olc.want: A legislative drafter writes bills. A drafter wants every key word defined and every reference checked. A drafter also wants every link to current law spelled out.
findings.S22.title: Each agency would decide if collecting data needs a warrant. No one checks when the agency says no.
findings.S22.plain: The bill would require a warrant, meaning permission from a judge, before the government searches a person's data. But the agency that wants the data would decide first if its own action counts as a search. It would also decide if one of the bill's exceptions applies, such as consent or an emergency. A judge would look at the matter only if the agency decided it needed a warrant. The bill requires no report or check when the agency decides it does not.
findings.S22.tech: The warrant rule gives an outside check for searches that reach a judge. But the agency doing the investigating decides if a case ever reaches a judge. That agency gains from reading the word "search" narrowly and the bill's exceptions broadly. A person can sue only after learning about the search. The bill does not require anyone to tell them.
findings.S22.use: An agency could decide that collecting someone's data needs no warrant under the surveillance bill. No judge, watchdog or member of the public would be told.
findings.S22.am.S22a.label: Yearly check of decisions not to seek a warrant
findings.S22.am.S22a.cost: This change would have each agency's Inspector General, its inside watchdog, check a sample of cases. These are cases where the agency collected data without a warrant. The checks would cost money. The public summary would need care so it does not reveal how investigations work. The President's branch of government picks these watchdogs. So their checks are less independent than a judge's review.
conflicts.0.claim: Under the surveillance bill, an agency that wants your data would decide for itself if it needs a warrant.
conflicts.0.detail: Each agency would decide if its own data collection counts as a search under the bill. It would also decide if one of the bill's exceptions applies. A judge would review a search only when the agency decided it needed a warrant and asked for one. The bill requires no report or check when the agency decides it does not.
conflicts.1.who: Each agency that does a search
conflicts.1.claim: The agency doing a search would decide if an emergency or a person's consent lets it skip the warrant.
conflicts.1.detail: Emergencies and consent are two of the bill's exceptions to the warrant rule. The agency that gains from an exception would decide if it applies. The bill requires no review after an agency relies on one.
conf_note: No conflicts involving named people have been looked into for this bill. It is not law, and it gives no job to a named official.
